summary: Harsha of the Pushyabhuti family, crowned king of Thanesar in 606, ruled the plains of northern India from Kannauj, with kings from Valabhi to Kamarupa accepting his overlordship. His drive south was stopped at the Narmada by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II in 618–19, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang left a vivid picture of his court. Harsha died without an heir in 647; a usurper seized Kannauj, and the empire fell apart.
details: Harsha's father Prabhakaravardhana ruled the small kingdom of Thanesar, north of Delhi, and died around 605. His elder son Rajyavardhana was soon killed by the king of Gauda (Bengal), usually identified as Shashanka, and in April 606 the sixteen-year-old Harsha was crowned. Older historians dated his conquests to 606–612, following the pilgrim Xuanzang's remark that he subdued the 'Five Indias', but the wars probably went on for years. Harsha made Kannauj (Kanyakubja) his capital. Rulers from Valabhi in the west to Kamarupa in the east came to accept his overlordship.

With the north under his control, Harsha looked south to the Deccan, ruled by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II. In the winter of 618–19 the two armies met on the banks of the Narmada river. Pulakeshin's Aihole inscription boasts that Harsha's joy 'melted away by fear' as his war elephants fell; a Chalukya grant dated April 619 already celebrates the victory. Harsha retreated, and the Narmada became the frontier between the two empires. Harsha's realm would stay a northern empire, never reaching into the Deccan.

Xuanzang, a Buddhist monk from Tang China, set out around 629 to find Buddhist texts at their source. He spent about thirteen years in India, roughly 630 to 644, travelling widely and studying at the great monastery of Nalanda under the teacher Shilabhadra. His later travel book, the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, is one of the main sources for Harsha's reign. Xuanzang describes Harsha as ruling from Kanyakubja (Kannauj) and praises his justice and generosity, though he wrote as an admiring guest.

Shashanka, king of Gauda in Bengal with his capital at Karnasuvarna, was Harsha's great enemy in the east, blamed for the death of Harsha's brother. To fight him, Harsha allied with Bhaskaravarman, king of Kamarupa (Assam). Harsha's attacks never broke Shashanka, who kept his kingdom until his death, dated about 636 (some sources say 625). His son Manava ruled for only eight months. Gauda was then divided between Harsha and Bhaskaravarman, carrying Harsha's power into Bengal.

Harsha opened diplomatic contact with the Tang dynasty of China by sending an envoy to its court. In reply, Emperor Taizong sent a mission in 643 led by Li Yibiao, with Wang Xuance as his assistant. The Chinese envoys met Harsha in Magadha, in what is now Bihar. The exchange linked Harsha's court with the Tang capital at Chang'an, a world away across the Himalayas. These contacts would bring Wang Xuance back to India a few years later, at a very different moment.

Harsha was a patron of Buddhism as well as of other faiths. Late in Xuanzang's stay, around 643, Harsha asked the pilgrim to come to Kannauj for a great Buddhist assembly. Kings of neighbouring states attended, together with Buddhist monks, Hindus and Jains. Harsha was by then an ally of Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa, whose court Xuanzang had just visited. The assembly showed off Harsha's power as overlord: subordinate kings came to his capital and joined his ceremonies, a sign of how far his authority reached.

After the Kannauj assembly, Harsha invited Xuanzang to the great gathering at Prayag (Allahabad), where the Ganges and Yamuna meet, a festival linked with the Kumbha Mela. Xuanzang watched the emperor hand out gifts on a huge scale to the poor and to religious men, an act of royal generosity Harsha was said to repeat every few years. Xuanzang then returned with him to Kannauj, received a grand farewell, and left for China, reaching Chang'an early in 645.

Harsha died in 647, possibly at Kannauj, aged about 57. He left no son, and the Pushyabhuti dynasty ended with him. A man named Arunasva usurped the throne of Kannauj. When a new Tang embassy under Wang Xuance arrived, Arunasva's forces attacked it, and Wang escaped overnight to Nepal. Without Harsha himself, the network of loyal and subordinate kings that held his empire together quickly dissolved, and northern India broke back into rival kingdoms.

From Nepal, Wang Xuance raised an army with the help of the Tibetan emperor Songtsen Gampo and the Nepalese king Narendradeva: about 1,200 Tibetan soldiers and more than 7,000 Nepalese cavalry. In 648 they attacked Arunasva at a place the Chinese called Chabuheluo. According to the Old Book of Tang the fighting lasted three days; Arunasva fled, was captured, and was taken back to China as a prisoner. The episode marked the end of Harsha's empire: no single power ruled the northern plains again for decades.
